c01.display: Welcome to unit five of NLP, Simply Explained. This is lesson 1: contextual embeddings, and a model called ELMo.
c01.spoken: Welcome to unit five of N L P, Simply Explained. This is lesson 1: contextual embeddings, and a model called ELMo.

c02.display: In unit four, every word got one vector. Today we fix the biggest problem with that idea.
c02.spoken: In unit four, every word got one vector. Today we fix the biggest problem with that idea.

c03.display: Here's the idea. The same word should get a different vector when it's used in a different sentence.
c03.spoken: Here's the idea. The same word should get a different vector when it's used in a different sentence.

c05.display: Static vectors, like Word2Vec's, give each word exactly one vector. "Bank" always gets the same one, whatever the sentence.
c05.spoken: Static vectors, like Word2Vec's, give each word exactly one vector. "Bank" always gets the same one, whatever the sentence.

c06.display: Contextual vectors give a word a fresh vector every time it's used, based on the sentence around it. So a river bank and a money bank get different vectors.
c06.spoken: Contextual vectors give a word a fresh vector every time it's used, based on the sentence around it. So a river bank and a money bank get different vectors.

c07.display: Here's the word "bank" in three sentences. A contextual model gives it three different vectors.
c07.spoken: Here's the word "bank" in three sentences. A contextual model gives it three different vectors.

c08.display: "We sat on the bank of the river": the side of a river.
c08.spoken: "We sat on the bank of the river": the side of a river.

c09.display: "I paid money into the bank": a place that keeps money.
c09.spoken: "I paid money into the bank": a place that keeps money.

c10.display: "Don't bank on it": here it's a verb, meaning to rely on something.
c10.spoken: "Don't bank on it": here it's a verb, meaning to rely on something.

c11.display: ELMo, from 2018, stands for embeddings from language models. Its word vectors come out of a deep language model built from LSTMs reading in both directions, so each vector depends on the whole sentence.
c11.spoken: ELMo, from 2018, stands for embeddings from language models. Its word vectors come out of a deep language model built from L S T ems reading in both directions, so each vector depends on the whole sentence.

c12.display: For "bank" in our first sentence, the vector is computed from everything around it: sat on the, of the river.
c12.spoken: For "bank" in our first sentence, the vector is computed from everything around it: sat on the, of the river.

c13.display: It's like asking someone what a word means while they're holding the whole sentence in mind.
c13.spoken: It's like asking someone what a word means while they're holding the whole sentence in mind.

c14.display: Here's how it works, in four steps.
c14.spoken: Here's how it works, in four steps.

c15.display: Pretrain: train two LSTM language models on a huge amount of plain text. One predicts the next word, reading forwards. The other predicts the previous word, reading backwards.
c15.spoken: Pretrain: train two LSTM language models on a huge amount of plain text. One predicts the next word, reading forwards. The other predicts the previous word, reading backwards.

c16.display: Read: run both models over your sentence.
c16.spoken: Read: run both models over your sentence.

c17.display: Mix: for each word, blend the outputs of their layers, using weights learned for your task.
c17.spoken: Mix: for each word, blend the outputs of their layers, using weights learned for your task.

c18.display: Plug in: feed these vectors into your own model, for tagging, question answering, or whatever you're building.
c18.spoken: Plug in: feed these vectors into your own model, for tagging, question answering, or whatever you're building.

c19.display: Why blend the layers? Because they learn different things.
c19.spoken: Why blend the layers? Because they learn different things.

c20.display: The lower layers capture more about grammar, like parts of speech.
c20.spoken: The lower layers capture more about grammar, like parts of speech.

c21.display: The higher layers capture more about meaning in context, like which sense of "bank" is meant.
c21.spoken: The higher layers capture more about meaning in context, like which sense of "bank" is meant.

c22.display: So each task can lean on the layers it needs most.
c22.spoken: So each task can lean on the layers it needs most.

c24.display: Adding its vectors improved results across many NLP tasks at once.
c24.spoken: Adding its vectors improved results across many N L P tasks at once.

c25.display: It proved that pretraining on plain, unlabelled text really pays off.
c25.spoken: It proved that pretraining on plain, unlabelled text really pays off.

c26.display: And it opened the door to BERT, our next and final lesson.
c26.spoken: And it opened the door to BERT, our next and final lesson.

c27.display: Quick quiz. What's the main difference between ELMo's vectors and Word2Vec's?
c27.spoken: Quick quiz. What's the main difference between ELMo's vectors and Word2Vec's?

c29.display: ELMo's vectors depend on the sentence. Word2Vec gives each word one fixed vector, but ELMo computes a new one every time the word is used.
c29.spoken: ELMo's vectors depend on the sentence. Word2Vec gives each word one fixed vector, but ELMo computes a new one every time the word is used.

c30.display: Let's recap. Static vectors give a word one vector, whatever the sentence.
c30.spoken: Let's recap. Static vectors give a word one vector, whatever the sentence.

c31.display: Contextual vectors change with the sentence, so "bank" can mean different things.
c31.spoken: Contextual vectors change with the sentence, so "bank" can mean different things.

c32.display: ELMo takes its vectors from a two-way LSTM language model, pretrained on lots of text.
c32.spoken: ELMo takes its vectors from a two-way LSTM language model, pretrained on lots of text.

c33.display: And it showed that pretraining on plain text pays off.
c33.spoken: And it showed that pretraining on plain text pays off.

c34.spoken: Next lesson: BERT. How did BERT learn language by filling in the blanks?
